title: The frame layer: window managers and agent multiplexers
summary:
The frame layer is about attention, not UI. People now run many long-lived coding agents across machines and worktrees, and these tools answer four questions: which agent needs me (per-pane status and an inbox), will it survive a disconnect or reboot (persistent sessions), can agents coordinate without me (socket APIs and CLIs for spawning, prompting and waiting), and where do I review (diffs, previews, PRs). There are two paths. Path A rebuilds the terminal multiplexer for agents: herdr (43k stars in six months), TUIOS, and the incumbents tmux and zellij, with Claude Squad as the first-wave ancestor. These run over SSH and own the PTYs, and what a pane shows is whatever program runs in it. Path B is the desktop agent workspace: the Codex app (inside the ChatGPT desktop app since 9 July 2026), Warp (client open-sourced 28 April 2026), cmux, Superset, Wave and Vibe Kanban (its company shut down in April 2026). These are steadily taking over the content layer with HTML or code: browsers you can comment on, Sites, MCP Apps, Pages, AI-written Go widgets. A status standard is emerging alongside: OSC 7501 (Rex/Superlogical; implemented by TUIOS, parsed by libghostty-vt), herdr's report-agent CLI, and OSC 9/99/777 notifications.

The open debates are terminal frame versus desktop frame, whether frames will eat the content layer, and whether a frame can be a business at all. In terminal frames the content layer is still unclaimed. herdr's plugin v1 is terminal-UI-only. TUIOS's ask-human (fixed-answer questions) and dock components (commands bound to cells) are the first small steps, and zellij's host-drawn components still come from compiled WASM. For fictty, the scope line holds: no frame lets an agent push a UI value, patch it by id, bind live data to it and read back its state. But exact text read-back is no longer unique, because herdr pane.read, zellij subscribe, tmux capture-pane and tuios screenshot --text all provide it. fictty's distinct claims are semantic state read-back, data that skips the model, and behaviour at frame rate. fictty should integrate rather than compete: emit OSC 7501 and OSC 9/777, report status to herdr, and ship recipes for herdr plugins, TUIOS popups, tmux 3.8 modal panes and zellij floating panes. It should build no frame features.

title: Terminal agent harnesses and the renderers under them
summary:
Terminal agent harnesses all rewrote or forked their renderers in the last 18 months: Claude Code moved off Ink to its own renderer and added a fullscreen mode with cell diffs. Codex draws with ratatui inline, sending history to native scrollback. opencode built OpenTUI (Zig core, Solid). Gemini CLI forked Ink and uses the alternate screen. Crush is on Bubble Tea v2 and Ultraviolet. pi built pi-tui, which diffs lines and wraps frames in synchronized output (DEC mode 2026). Flicker, scrollback and memory are now solved problems, but each team solved them separately. On the question of who else may draw inside the harness, they split three ways. Claude Code (mods, on by default since v2.1.287, 1 Oct 2026), opencode (TUI plugins, since March 2026) and pi (ctx.ui extensions) open their screens to third-party code: JS/TS returning element trees or lines, loaded as plugins. Codex and Google send rich visuals elsewhere. Codex writes HTML and opens it in a browser or the desktop app, and draws Mermaid as text. Google moved consumers from Gemini CLI to the closed Go Antigravity CLI, tied to a desktop app, on 19 May 2026. Crush and Gemini CLI let nobody draw. Two corrections to the first landscape post: Google's flagship terminal agent is now closed and tied to a desktop app, and pi (114k stars) belongs in the table.

Underneath, every harness is solving two things: a person has to watch and steer a long-running agent without the screen fighting them, and the transcript isn't enough for diffs, plans, approvals and status. The open debates are inline vs fullscreen (Codex keeps native scrollback; the rest rebuild scrolling, search and selection), code vs data for in-harness UI (every harness that opened its screen chose code), and whether the terminal is the display or only the control surface (OpenAI and Google are moving the display to desktop apps; Anthropic invests in both). No harness offers a UI runtime fictty could adopt instead of building one: none takes a UI as data from the agent, none gives the model exact read-back, and the closest options are either locked to one harness or written in another language. The real threat is Claude Code mods as a substitute for Claude Code users. A 200-line mod, or a first-party 'draw this JSON' mod, covers much of fictty's job inside the harness where most of its users live. fictty's defensible ground is everything outside one harness, exact read-back, frame rate and replay. The recommended path is to build fictty and bridge into harnesses that allow it, starting with a Claude Code mod that draws a fictty value in a pane and exposes a screen tool.

title: TUI frameworks fictty could build on or adopt
summary:
TUI frameworks solve how a developer writes a terminal app that ships. Their 2025–26 work was mostly renderers, because the streaming coding agents needed them. Bubble Tea v2 got the Cursed Renderer on Ultraviolet. OpenTUI is a Zig core under React and Solid, written for opencode. ratatui 0.30 split into modular crates and is what Codex draws with. Ink v8 added incremental line rendering, but Claude Code still replaced Ink's renderer with its own. I see six paths. (1) The Elm loop: Bubble Tea, tui-realm, Raxol and fictty. (2) React in the terminal: Ink, OpenTUI's bindings, iocraft. (3) The web's architecture in cells: Textual, with a DOM, CSS and a browser via textual-serve. Textual's company folded in 2025 and one person now maintains it. (4) A native core under a scripting API. (5) Specs over code: GitHub's TUIKit, where an LLM compiles Markdown specs into four frameworks. (6) One app on many surfaces: Textual-serve, Raxol to LiveView, SSH and MCP, Wish and OpenTUI over SSH, Ratzilla to WASM. Agents appear in these frameworks only as authors of code (OpenTUI ships an agent skill) and, newly, as status reporters. Bubble Tea v2.1 added OSC 7501 on 8 Oct 2026. That protocol is Superlogical's, written for its Rex terminal, not TUIOS's as our first post said.

The gap is the same in every framework. The UI is code, its state lives in the language's heap, and read-back is a test helper (teatest, lastFrame, captureCharFrame, Pilot), not a live interface. Raxol is the partial exception: it derives MCP tools from the component tree. But it has 80 stars and one maintainer, and it is still code-first. The open debates are code vs data, flexbox vs constraints (agents expect flexbox), whether the renderer is a moat (it is becoming a commodity), and accessibility (nobody has solved it; Ink has a crude linear mode, and TUIKit puts roles in the spec). The verdict is to stay on ratatui. Its immediate mode matches fictty's pure view and its one-source-of-truth rule, and Ratzilla gives a browser surface that reuses the same view code. OpenTUI is the only alternative substrate worth revisiting, and only if fictty starts rebuilding its code, diff and markdown views, images, SSH or embedded terminal. No framework in this cluster replaces fictty's actual work: the UI as one serializable value, patch by id, data sources, the socket and exact read-back. The real threats sit in other clusters: data-format renderers growing a live loop, and HTML artifacts.

title: Agent-generated UI in the terminal: the closest neighbours
summary:
Agent-generated UI in the terminal splits into two groups. The first is about how an agent puts something in front of a person and gets an answer back. Projects take five paths. Prebuilt canvases: claude-canvas had about 1,500 stars within a week, then was abandoned as an unsupported proof of concept. A format plus a terminal renderer shipped as a library: json-render's Ink renderer, the Rust a2ui crate on ratatui, a2ui-ink and a2tea, so A2UI now renders in a terminal in three languages. UI drawn inline in the agent's own chat: a2tea's Crush fork and json-render's ink-chat example. A workspace the agent drives: Laura, which tiles panes of files, diffs and logs by pane id over a socket and returns the person's inline review to the chat. Code-first frameworks with an agent surface: Raxol derives MCP tools from its component tree, and Melker makes apps permissioned, readable documents. The second group is about how an agent uses a screen it didn't write. There has been a flood of near-identical PTY drivers in 2026 (tui-use, pilotty, two unrelated agent-tuis, agent-tty and others), alongside older MCP servers (tmux-mcp, iterm-mcp, terminalcp, ht), Microsoft's tui-test rewritten in Rust with Playwright-style locators, and VHS for recording. The best drivers try to recover structure: ConductorOne's agent-tui adds roles and refs through per-program adapters ("A terminal program is already a state machine. The problem is that the state is presented as a screen.").

The real problem underneath is that an agent needs a screen it understands. The open debate has four questions. Where should generated UI live: inline in the chat, in a split beside it, or in a browser? Is the format the product or the runtime? Should structure be retrofitted onto any program or published by the screen itself? Should UI values allow logic (json-render's $cond and $computed, Melker's handlers) or stay pure data (A2UI, fictty)? The format question is close to settled, and fictty doesn't own it. The runtime question has almost no takers. No one else offers a long-lived screen an outside agent can attach to, push to, patch by id, drive and read back exactly, with data bound to commands. Laura comes closest but only arranges documents; the format renderers have the values but no loop. That position is real but narrow. Three concrete risks: json-render or A2UI could ship an attachable terminal host; big agents could render UI inline; drivers could prove good enough for most tasks.

title: The HTML camp: agents write pages
summary:
The HTML camp starts from one observation: a UI used to be expensive, so agents answered in text, and now a purpose-built interface costs one model turn. Its members bet that the model (or a developer) writes HTML/JS and a host renders it in a sandbox. The camp follows five paths. (1) The model writes the page and the host keeps it: Claude Artifacts, Claude Code Artifacts, Gemini dynamic view and AI Mode generative UI, and the short Imagine with Claude demo. (2) The developer writes a reviewed template and the model only calls it: MCP Apps/MCP-UI and the OpenAI Apps SDK, which converged on MCP Apps in February 2026. (3) The model writes code against a fixed catalogue: Cursor Canvas's component library, and Claude's Slides/Docs/Design/Dashboards templates from September 2026. (4) A local review loop around agent HTML: Lavish, with element-level annotations and a long poll. (5) The model writes durable apps: v0. Under all of them sit three problems. Text flattens spatial and interactive information. People increasingly use generated UI to understand things (explainers, module maps, simulations; Google's research found raters strongly preferred generated pages to text, speed aside). And a page the person can't answer through is only a broadcast, so 2026 was the year of return paths: Artifact comments sent to a watching Claude session, Lavish's poll, MCP Apps' update-model-context, ChatGPT widget state.

The open debate is code versus data, and the camp's own behaviour is drifting toward data for recurring shapes. Anthropic added typed templates, Cursor constrains output to a component library, MCP Apps fixes templates ahead of time, Google pairs free-form HTML for consumers with A2UI for developers, and OpenAI dropped Canvas from GPT-5.5 (28 May 2026) in favour of inline blocks. In most of the camp, data is frozen into the page at write time. Live data arrives only through vendor proxies (claude.ai connectors, MCP tool calls), never from local commands. Read-back is source code, DOM snapshots or app-chosen context, never the exact rendered frame. For fictty, the honest finding is that Claude Code Artifacts, with comments-to-Claude, watching, connector data and a shared database, now covers a real share of the ten-minute working screens fictty targets, for anyone with a browser and a claude.ai login. fictty should not build hosting, sharing or HTML review. It should export to HTML and hand off. It should compete only where the camp is absent: local live data at frame rate, exact frame read-back, runtime-owned behaviour, any agent, in the pane over SSH. Corrections to the first pass: ChatGPT Canvas is gone from current models, and Cursor Canvas (missed) belongs here.

title: The data camp: agents fill in declarative UI
summary:
The data camp is solving one problem: letting a model put interactive UI in front of a person without the host running code the model wrote. Every entry uses server-driven UI. The host keeps a catalogue of trusted components and draws them its own way, and the model sends a description. Adaptive Cards did this for bots in 2017. A2UI, json-render, OpenUI, ChatKit widgets and Tambo redo it for agents under three new pressures: streaming (flat lists with ids, or JSON Patch lines, so a half-sent UI still draws), tokens (OpenUI's terse language, and A2UI's Express proposal following it), and editing over several turns (everything addressable by id or name). The paths split five ways. A2UI and Adaptive Cards bet on a portable format where the host owns the look. json-render is a toolkit that treats formats as catalogues and has many renderers, including the only real terminal one (Ink). OpenUI is a compact language with variables, logic and model-free data queries, plus a paid gateway. AG-UI and CopilotKit own the transport and shared state and stay neutral on format. The AI SDK, ChatKit and Tambo follow "model picks, developer renders". Almost everything lives in a browser chat and treats the UI as a message, not a standing screen.

The open debates: how much logic belongs in the data (every "safe like data" format has added conditions or functions, and OpenUI went all the way to a language); JSON or a terser syntax; whether catalogues make every UI look the same; and standard or toolkit. Consolidation has begun. Thesys renamed C1 to OpenUI Cloud, OpenAI is retiring Agent Builder on 30 November 2026, Tambo Cloud shuts down on 31 October 2026, and the AI SDK moved streamUI back to experimental. Nobody in the camp offers exact read-back of what was drawn, a long-running screen an outside agent attaches to, or (apart from OpenUI's Query) data that skips the model. Verdict on adopting a format: none replaces fictty's value. A2UI is the only one worth speaking natively, as an input adapter once v1.0 is stable. json-render contributes a patch dialect (RFC 6902/7396), OpenUI contributes data-source details, and AG-UI could be a second transport. The camp says almost nothing about throwaway screens built to help a person understand something; that framing is open.

title: Ideas: disposable UI, malleable software, and learning by seeing
summary:
For forty years a UI was durable and costly: a team built it once and many people used it. In 2025 and 2026 it became something a model writes in a minute for one person and one question. This cluster covers the responses, which split into eight paths. (1) Malleable and home-cooked software (Ink & Switch, Sloan, Appleton) says regenerating apps is not the goal. People need to adapt and compose durable tools over shared data, and "AI code generation alone does not address all the barriers". (2) Per-prompt generated UI (Google Generative UI, Claude inline visuals): the labs' default is HTML written per answer and thrown away. Google's raters preferred it to markdown 83 to 91% of the time, with a wait of a minute or more hidden from them. Anthropic now draws a line in its product between permanent Artifacts and "temporary" visuals built "to aid understanding". (3) Catalogues (ChatGPT's roughly 70 concept modules, which is our inference; NotebookLM's fixed formats; Gemini's retrieved diagrams and quizzes): where correctness matters, labs pick fixed formats that the model fills in. (4) Instruments for understanding (Geoffrey Litt): when agents write the code, understanding is the bottleneck, and HUDs beat copilots. His examples are a one-minute custom debugger, a migration command center, and an explainer with a quiz. (5) The explorable-explanation craft (Victor, Case, Distill, manim) was right but too costly to author: Distill stopped in 2021 after editors spent 50+ hours on single articles. Agents now cut that cost, though generated visuals still have layout errors. (6) Reactive notebooks driven by agents (Observable, marimo pair). marimo pair puts the agent inside a live kernel where it reads values back exactly, which is the closest loop to fictty's. (7) Tutors, mostly in text. The evidence says behaviour design matters more than the model or the medium: Bastani found unguarded help harms learning, Kestin found a guarded tutor can beat a class, and Khanmigo's two-year trial shows 0.04 SD. Learning science backs relevant pictures plus words (g=0.37) and simulations for transfer. It warns that decorative visuals hurt and rejects "visual learners". No study tests a generated interactive screen against a text tutor. (8) The medium fight: Ptacek argues cheap UI means native apps, not TUIs. The replies point to remote use, Jane Street's finding that text snapshots make agents better at UI, and joshka's semantic-protocol idea, which Ptacek himself calls the strongest rebuttal.

What is really being solved is the gap between what the computer knows and what the person understands, at the moment they need it. The open debate is about three things: who owns the interface's lifecycle (vendor, user, or the model for a minute), how it is checked (designer, schema, or nothing), and whether it changes understanding or only preference. Three findings cut across the cluster. Preference is not learning. Data/catalogue approaches win where correctness matters. Live state plus exact read-back is becoming the requirement. fictty should not pitch itself as an education product, because the browser and the labs own rich general explanation. Its defensible ground is instruments for understanding what an agent is doing, in the terminal where the agent works: bound to live sources, read back exactly, with checkpoints where the person predicts or answers.
